grammar: Marks the topic of speaking, thinking or writing rather than a target of an action.
日本の歴史について調べています。
将来について話し合いました。
change up to now; movement toward
Marks change reaching the present or movement toward the viewpoint; context determines the sense.
少しずつ暖かくなってきました。
犬がこちらへ走ってきました。
A dog came running toward us.
Choice depends on the following predicate; do not assume complete interchangeability.
子供が走っているのを見ました。
動詞辞書形ことができる
Explicit ability or possibility; teach before contrasting inflected potential forms.
ここで切符を買うことができます。
妹は漢字を読むことができます。
My younger sister can read kanji.
Teach godan, ichidan and irregular formation; potential forms do not express permission by themselves.
私は百メートル泳げます。
I can swim one hundred metres.
この席から海が見られます。
You can see the sea from this seat.
Often presents the reason more softly or objectively; nouns and na-adjectives need their linking form.
電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました。
I was late because the train was delayed.
静かなので、この部屋で勉強します。
I study in this room because it is quiet.
動詞なければならない
A double-negative obligation pattern; also teach less formal spoken reductions through listening.
明日までに払わなければなりません。
今日は早く帰らなければなりません。
I must go home early today.
Attach to a verb stem or adjective stem; evaluate against a contextual standard.
昨日は食べすぎました。
この靴は小さすぎます。
Quote a plain predicate; distinguish speaker opinion from independently verified information.
明日は晴れると思います。
I think it will be sunny tomorrow.
この方法がいいと思います。
I think this method is good.
Extend the progressive beyond ongoing actions; intransitive change verbs often describe a resulting state.
私は東京に住んでいます。
Use with nouns and nominal predicates; Japanese usually omits recoverable pronouns.
not be a noun; polite negation
Formal negative copula; introduce the common conversational contraction as a later variation.
これは私の傘ではありません。
父は医者ではありません。
My father is not a doctor.
Add the question particle to a polite sentence; teach who, what, when and where through vocabulary.
The topic particle is pronounced wa; contrast topic with the grammatical subject.
私は大阪に住んでいます。
Use for the answer to a who-or-what question and with existence predicates.
The object particle is normally pronounced o; it follows the affected object.
The first noun narrows or identifies the second; not all uses express ownership.
これは母のかばんです。
Usually replaces the topic or subject particle in elementary affirmative clauses.
at a place where an action happens
Contrast action location with the location of existence.
家で昼ご飯を食べます。
an inanimate thing exists at a place
Use for things and plants; not the ordinary existence predicate for people or animals.
机の上に本があります。
There is a book on the desk.
There is a tree in the garden.
a person or animal exists at a place
Use for people and animals; teach location and subject word order together.
There are children in the park.
There is a cat in the room.
go to; move toward a destination
The directional particle written he is pronounced e; destination and purpose are distinct.
I will go to Kyoto tomorrow.
I go to school every day.
by; using a means or instrument
Contrast instrument or transport with action-location uses of the same particle.
電車で会社に行きます。
I go to work by train.
ペンで名前を書きます。
I write my name with a pen.
Specific clock times and dates commonly take this particle; relative time words often do not.
月曜日に会いましょう。
Also introduces a companion, but distinguish that function in practice.
I will buy bread and eggs.
I have an older brother and an older sister.
Standalone demonstrative pronouns; choose by physical or conversational distance.
これは新しい時計です。
あれは私の自転車です。
That over there is my bicycle.
this noun; that noun; that noun over there
These demonstratives require a following noun.
そのかばんは重いですか。
The adjective itself inflects: negative in -kunai and past in -katta; do not attach a plain copula.
Use the linking na before nouns, not directly before the polite copula.
静かな部屋が好きです。
Can describe a habit or a future event; teach verb groups and dictionary-form lookup together.
Use for a negative habit or intention; the temporal context determines English tense.
I will not go out today.
動詞ました／ませんでした
polite past verb; polite negative past verb
Teach past affirmative and negative as a contrastive pair.
今朝は走りませんでした。
I did not run this morning.
A direct polite request; appropriateness depends on relationship and burden.
ここに名前を書いてください。
At this stage teach ongoing action; resulting states need separate instruction later.
今、夕飯を作っています。
弟はテレビを見ています。
My younger brother is watching television.
may do; it is acceptable to do
Requests permission when used as a question; not the same as ability.
ここに座ってもいいですか。
この辞書を使ってもいいです。
Requires the plain negative form; scaffold that form before using the request.
窓を開けないでください。
Please do not open the window.
ここで走らないでください。
Attach to the polite-verb stem; generally states the speaker's desire or asks the listener's.
I want to go to Japan.
今日は早く寝たいです。
I want to go to bed early today.
Use for the speaker's desire; avoid reporting another person's internal state without evidence.
新しい辞書が欲しいです。
would you like to do; invitation
A negative question can make an invitation rather than asking about a negative fact.
一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
Would you like to have lunch together?
週末、映画を見ませんか。
Would you like to watch a film this weekend?
Use for joint action; do not translate every instance as a command.
after doing; first do and then
The first event must precede the second; teach a practical sequence.
宿題をしてから遊びます。
I play after doing my homework.
朝ご飯を食べてから出かけました。
I went out after eating breakfast.
A is more adjective than B
The comparison baseline follows the comparative particle; adjective forms do not become comparative.
このかばんはあのかばんより軽いです。
This bag is lighter than that bag.
今日は昨日より暖かいです。
do something and then do something
Conjoins actions; teach te-form sound changes by verb group, including irregular verbs.
駅で切符を買って、電車に乗りました。
I bought a ticket at the station and boarded the train.
家に帰って、夕飯を作ります。
I will go home and make dinner.
Teach common object, person and age counters with their sound changes, not one universal counter.
りんごを三つ買いました。
go in order to do something
Attach to the polite-verb stem; motion is part of the meaning.
本を借りに図書館へ行きます。
I go to the library to borrow books.
友達に会いに行きました。
I went to meet a friend.
like a thing; be good at a thing
These are adjectival predicates, not transitive verbs; avoid praising one's own skill insensitively.
My older sister is good at cooking.
Sentence-final particles convey stance; tone matters, so do not treat them as interchangeable decoration.
It is hot today, isn't it?
It is the next station, you know.
What about N?; a contextual follow-up question
The predicate is omitted when it is understood from context.
everyone in a group shares the predicate
みんな comes before the predicate; for example, 私たちはみんな学生です。
very; an intensifier placed before an adjective
a little; somewhat, placed before an adjective
Often used for a mildly unpleasant state, as in ちょっと寒いです.
feel that something is a certain way
と marks the impression; 感じます is the polite form of 感じる.
時間表現＋（は）＋主語＋動詞／主語＋時間表現＋動詞
Put a time expression before the action, either before or after the subject.
For example, 今日、働きます and 午後、料理します. Relative time expressions such as 今日 usually do not need に.
Use に to mark the destination with 着きます.
Put a length of time before the verb.
For example, 五分休みます means “rest for five minutes.”
欲しい changes to 欲しくないです: “do not want.”
a small amount of a noun
少し expresses a small quantity; for example, ご飯が少し欲しいです。
For example, 授業の前に means before class.
Use a number with 号室 for a numbered room, or 番 for a numbered label.
For example, 三号室 means “room number three,” and 三番 can identify a numbered place.
For example, 八時半 means half past eight.
Use にいます to say where a person is.
There is/are; have something or someone.
Use が with あります for things and います for people or animals. For possession, the possessor can be the topic: 私は友達がいます。
N1はN2にN3をあげます／くれます
give something to someone; use くれます when the recipient is the speaker or the speaker's group
Use に for the recipient and を for the thing given.
form numbers from 11 to 19 by combining ten and the ones digit; larger tens follow the same pattern
For example, 十五 is fifteen.
何＋助数詞＋Nですか／どれくらい＋Nですか
ask how many with a counter, or ask how much/how long with どれくらい
Use 何冊 for books, 何杯 for cups, and どれくらい for an amount such as water.
describe a location as behind, in front of, or beside a noun
Japanese uses separate positional words after の, rather than a location suffix. Use に with います or あります to say something is at that location.
An i-adjective directly modifies a noun.
For example, 新しい服 means “new clothes.”
Mark the person being spoken to with に.
For example, きれいです means it looks beautiful or attractive.
Use に for the person who receives the kindness.
変化を表す文＋ました／ています
Report a new situation or a resulting state using the Japanese form that fits the verb.
Japanese has no general sentence-final particle for this meaning. For example, use 降り始めました for rain starting, or ついています for a light or television being on.
本当に comes before an adjective, as in 本当においしいです.
Add たち to a person or animal noun to refer to a group.
For example, 先生たち and 犬たち. Japanese often uses this suffix where Chinese uses a plural ending.
do something again at a later time
また can come before the verb for a future or intended repetition.
there is not; do not have
Use the polite negative of あります to say something is absent or not available.
Form weekday names with 曜日.
Japanese weekday names are not formed by adding a number.
場所に住みます／住んでいます
Live or stay at a place; mark the place with に.
Make a number in the hundreds by putting the remaining number after 百.
Japanese usually omits 一 before 百, as in 百円.
Make a number in the thousands by putting the remaining number after 千.
Japanese usually omits 一 before 千, as in 千円.
と marks the person accompanying the subject.
A polite way to request an item, as in パンを一切れください。
どのくらい＋形容詞ですか
Ask how + adjective, such as how big or how tall.
どれくらい can also be used in place of どのくらい.
Keep the object before the verb; mark tense on the verb ending.
Japanese does not split a verb-object expression to insert aspect or quantity.
which one or ones; which + noun
Use どの before a noun to ask which item or items.
Use an い-adjective adverbially before a verb.
For example, 早い becomes 早く.
A plain-form verb can modify a noun, as in “the shop she opened.”
Use the plain form directly before the noun; the main sentence can still be polite.
Use の to connect the event or noun to 後; に can mark when the next action happens.
describe a location relative to N1
の links the place to its landmark; に can mark the location with あります or います.
Place どうやって before the action.
Give a date in year-month-day order, putting each number before 年, 月, or 日.
The reading of 日 varies for some dates, such as ついたち and みっか.
Ask how something is or what it is like.
Put the topic before は; use どうですか to ask for an opinion or description.
Ordinal number before a noun, formed with a number, counter, and 目
For example, 二冊目の本 means “the second book,” and 三日目 means “the third day.”
千＋一の位（十・百の位が0の場合）
In Japanese, a number such as 1,008 is read 千八, omitting the zero places.
For example, 千八円（せんはちえん）.
Put 半分 after a container to say half a container of something.
For example, 牛乳をコップ半分飲みます.
ありがとう＋ございます
Use ございます after ありがとう to express thanks politely.
Use 歳 after the number of years; add です for a polite sentence.
Use 杯 as a counter for drinks; the reading varies with the number.
Connect a negative verb form to a following description or feeling.
For example, いる becomes いなくて in 家族がいなくて寂しいです。
Ask an open question with a question word such as who, what, where, or when.
Use a question word in the answer slot and finish the polite question with か.
Ask a question by putting a question word in the answer position; do not add a separate yes-no question marker.
Use with question words such as 誰, 何, and どこ. The polite question ending か may still be used.
Come somewhere in order to do something.
Put the verb stem for the purpose before に来ます.
A plain negative verb modifies a noun.
Use the negative plain form of a verb before a noun to describe someone or something that does not do the action.
引用する語句＋と＋言います
Put と after a quoted word or phrase before 言います.
Use と to mark the words being said.
い形容詞くありません
Polite negative form of an い-adjective
Replace the adjective ending い with くありません.
い形容詞語幹＋すぎます
Attach すぎます to an い-adjective stem to say that something is too much or excessive.
もう precedes a negative predicate.
A natural expression for saying something is ready.
Mark the place where an action or posture happens with に.
Use for a location such as そこに座る; this is not the time-point に.
Say that something is acceptable or will do using Nで大丈夫です.

Tell the time using the hour and, when needed, the minutes.
Put the time of day before the hour. Use 時 after the hour and 分 after the minutes.
Use つ as a general counter for things.
After a number, つ counts things when no more specific counter is used.
Get on or take a vehicle; mark the vehicle with に.
Use に with a vehicle when saying that someone gets on or takes it.
Meet someone; に marks the person you meet.
Use に after the person you meet.
Get on or board a vehicle; mark the vehicle with に.
Use に before 乗る for vehicles such as a car, train, or airplane.
A call comes in for someone.
Use に to mark the person receiving an incoming call.
A numbered day; the nth day.
日目 marks a day in a sequence. 三日目 is read みっかめ.
